entries.047c1081a41890c43ac160f5c3ee1cacccc9f0c2: <div sID="gen30599" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Rom.7" sID="Rom.7"/> <div eID="gen30599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30600" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30601" type="x-p"/> We may observe in this chapter, I. Our freedom from the law further urged as an argument to press upon us sanctification, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.1-Rom.7.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. The excellency and usefulness of the law asserted and proved from the apostle's own experience, notwithstanding, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7-Rom.7.14">ver. 7-14</reference>. III. A description of the conflict between grace and corruption in the heart, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.14-Rom.7.25">ver. 14, 15, to the end</reference>.
entries.df159bd05fb89b90b7403f2d84879b62714ca9d6: <div eID="gen30601" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30600" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Observations Respecting the Law. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30602" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Know ye not, brethren, (for I speak to them that know the law,) how that the law hath dominion over a man as long as he liveth? <hi type="super">2</hi> For the woman which hath a husband is bound by the law to <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband so long as he liveth; but if the husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband. <hi type="super">3</hi> So then if, while <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband liveth, she be married to another man, she shall be called an adulteress: but if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man. <hi type="super">4</hi> Wherefore, my brethren, ye also are become dead to the law by the body of Christ; that ye should be married to another, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to him who is raised from the dead, that we should bring forth fruit unto God. <hi type="super">5</hi> For when we were in the flesh, the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death. <hi type="super">6</hi> But now we are delivered from the law, that being dead wherein we were held; that we should serve in newness of spirit, and not <hi type="italic">in</hi> the oldness of the letter. <div eID="gen30602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30603" type="x-p"/> Among other arguments used in the foregoing chapter to persuade us against sin, and to holiness, this was one (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.14">v. 14</reference>), that <hi type="italic">we are not under the law;</hi> and this argument is here further insisted upon and explained (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">We are delivered from the law.</hi> What is meant by this? And how is it an argument why sin should not reign over us, and why we should walk in newness of life? 1. We are delivered from the power of the law which curses and condemns us for the sin committed by us. The sentence of the law against us is vacated and reversed, by the death of Christ, to all true believers. The law saith, <hi type="italic">The soul that sins shall die;</hi> but we are delivered from the law. <hi type="italic">The Lord has taken away thy sin, thou shalt not die.</hi> We are <hi type="italic">redeemed from the curse of the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.13">Gal. iii. 13</reference>. 2. We are delivered from that power of the law which irritates and provokes the sin that dwelleth in us. This the apostle seems especially to refer to (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The motions of sins which were by the law.</hi> The law, by commanding, forbidding, threatening, corrupt and fallen man, but offering no grace to cure and strengthen, did but stir up the corruption, and, like the sun shining upon a dunghill, excite and draw up the filthy steams. We being lamed by the fall, the law comes and directs us, but provides nothing to heal and help our lameness, and so makes us halt and stumble the more. Understand this of the law not as a rule, but as a covenant of works. Now each of these is an argument why we should be holy; for here is encouragement to endeavours, though in many things we come short. We are under grace, which promises strength to do what it commands, and pardon upon repentance when we do amiss. This is the scope of these verses in general, that, in point of profession and privilege, we are under a covenant of grace, and not under a covenant of works—under the gospel of Christ, and not under the law of Moses. The difference between a law-state and a gospel-state he had before illustrated by the similitude of rising to a new life, and serving a new master; now here he speaks of is under the similitude of being married to a new husband. <div eID="gen30603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30604" type="x-p"/> I. Our first marriage was to the law, which, according to the law of marriage, was to continue only during the life of the law. The law of marriage is binding till the death of one of the parties, no matter which, and no longer. The death of either discharges both. For this he appeals to themselves, as persons knowing the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I speak to those that know the law.</hi> It is a great advantage to discourse with those that have knowledge, for such can more readily understand and apprehend a truth. Many of the Christians at Rome were such as had been Jews, and so were well acquainted with the law. One has some hold of knowing people. <hi type="italic">The law hath power over a man as long as he liveth;</hi> in particular, the law of marriage hath power; or, in general, every law is so limited—the laws of nations, of relations, of families, &c. 1. The obligation of laws extends no further; by death the servant who, while he lived, was under the yoke, is <hi type="italic">freed from his master,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.3.19">Job iii. 19</reference>. 2. The condemnation of laws extends no further; death is the finishing of the law. <hi type="italic">Actio moritur cum person&#226;—The action expires with the person.</hi> The severest laws could but kill the body, and after that there is no more that they can do. Thus while we were alive to the law we were under the power of it—while we were in our Old-Testament state, before the gospel came into the world, and before it came with power into our hearts. Such is the law of marriage (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.2">v. 2</reference>), the woman is bound to her husband during life, so bound to him that she cannot marry another; if she do, she shall be reckoned an adulteress, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.3">v. 3</reference>. It will make her an adulteress, not only to be defiled by, but to be married to, another man; for that is so much the worse, upon this account, that it abuses an ordinance of God, by making it to patronise the uncleanness. Thus were we married to the law (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">When we were in the flesh,</hi> that is, in a carnal state, under the reigning power of sin and corruption—in the flesh as in our element—then <hi type="italic">the motions of sins which were by the law did work in our members,</hi> we were carried down the stream of sin, and the law was but as an imperfect dam, which made the stream to swell the higher, and rage the more. Our desire was towards sin, as that of the wife towards her husband, and sin ruled over us. We embraced it, loved it, devoted all to it, conversed daily with it, made it our care to please it. We were under a law of sin and death, as the wife under the law of marriage; and the product of this marriage was fruit brought forth unto death, that is, actual transgressions were produced by the original corruption, such as deserve death. Lust, having conceived by the law (which is the strength of sin, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.56">1 Cor. xv. 56</reference>), <hi type="italic">bringeth forth sin, and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">Jam. i. 15</reference>. This is the posterity that springs from this marriage to sin and the law. This comes of the motions of sin working in our members. And this continues during life, while the law is alive to us, and we are alive to the law. <div eID="gen30604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30605" type="x-p"/> II. Our second marriage is to Christ: and how comes this about? Why, <div eID="gen30605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30606" type="x-p"/> 1. We are freed, by death, from our obligation to the law as a covenant, as the wife is from her obligation to her husband, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.3">v. 3</reference>. This resemblance is not very close, nor needed it to be. <hi type="italic">You are become dead to the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">v. 4</reference>. He does not say, "The law is dead" (some think because he would avoid giving offence to those who were yet zealous for the law), but, which comes all to one, <hi type="italic">You are dead to the law.</hi> As the crucifying of the world to us, and of us to the world, amounts to one and the same thing, so doth the law dying, and our dying to it. We are <hi type="italic">delivered from the law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">katergethemen</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">we are nulled</hi> as to the law; our obligation to it as a husband is cassated and made void. And then he speaks of the law being dead as far as it was a law of bondage to us: <hi type="italic">That being dead wherein we were held;</hi> not the law itself, but its obligation to punishment and its provocation to sin. It is dead, it has lost its power; and this (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">v. 4</reference>) <hi type="italic">by the body of Christ,</hi> that is, by the sufferings of Christ in his body, by his crucified body, which abrogated the law, answered the demands of it, made satisfaction for our violation of it, purchased for us a covenant of grace, in which righteousness and strength are laid up for us, such as were not, nor could be, by the law. We are dead to the law by our union with the mystical body of Christ. By being incorporated into Christ in our baptism professedly, in our believing powerfully and effectually, we are dead to the law, have no more to do with it than the dead servant, that is free from his master, hath to do with his master's yoke. <div eID="gen30606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30607" type="x-p"/> 2. We are married to Christ. The day of our believing is the day of our espousals to the Lord Jesus. We enter upon a life of dependence on him and duty to him: <hi type="italic">Married to another, even to him who is raised from the dead,</hi> a periphrasis of Christ and very pertinent here; for as our dying to sin and the law is in conformity to the death of Christ, and the crucifying of his body, so our devotedness to Christ in newness of life is in conformity to the resurrection of Christ. We are married to the raised exalted Jesus, a very honourable marriage. Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2 Cor. xi. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.29">Eph. v. 29</reference>. Now we are thus married to Christ, (1.) <hi type="italic">That we should bring forth fruit unto God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">v. 4</reference>. One end of marriage is fruitfulness: God instituted the ordinance that he might seek a <hi type="italic">godly seed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.15">Mal. ii. 15</reference>. The wife is compared to the fruitful vine, and children are called the fruit of the womb. Now the great end of our marriage to Christ is our fruitfulness in love, and grace, and every good work. This is fruit unto God, pleasing to God, according to his will, aiming at his glory. As our old marriage to sin produced fruit unto death, so our second marriage to Christ produces fruit unto God, fruits of righteousness. Good works are the children of the new nature, the products of our union with Christ, as the fruitfulness of the vine is the product of its union with the root. Whatever our professions and pretensions may be, there is no fruit brought forth to God till we are married to Christ; it is in Christ Jesus that we are created unto good works, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Eph. ii. 10</reference>. The only fruit which turns to a good account is that which is brought forth in Christ. This distinguishes the good works of believers from the good works of hypocrites and self-justifiers that they are brought forth in marriage, done in union with Christ, in the name of the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="Col.3.17">Col. iii. 17</reference>. This is, without controversy, one of the great mysteries of godliness. (2.) <hi type="italic">That we should serve in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.6">v. 6</reference>. Being married to a new husband, we must change our way. Still we must serve, but it is a service that is perfect freedom, whereas the service of sin was a perfect drudgery: we must now serve in newness of spirit, by new spiritual rules, from new spiritual principles, in spirit and in truth, <reference osisRef="John.4.24">John iv. 24</reference>. There must be a renovation of our spirits wrought by the spirit of God, and in that we must serve. <hi type="italic">Not in the oldness of the letter;</hi> that is, we must not rest in mere external services, as the carnal Jews did, who gloried in their adherence to the letter of the law, and minded not the spiritual part of worship. The letter is said to kill with its bondage and terror, but we are delivered from that yoke that we may serve God without fear, in holiness and righteousness, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>. We are under the dispensation of the Spirit, and therefore must be spiritual, and serve in the spirit. Compare with this <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3">2 Cor. iii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">6</reference>, &c. It becomes us to worship within the veil, and no longer in the outward court.
entries.e45c22951c6c77e9f2beb4f7af1620ce3ea09996: <div eID="gen30607" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Excellency of the Law; Usefulness of the Law. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 58.)</title> <div sID="gen30608" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> What shall we say then? <hi type="italic">Is</hi> the law sin? God forbid. Nay, I had not known sin, but by the law: for I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet. <hi type="super">8</hi> But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. For without the law sin <hi type="italic">was</hi> dead. 9 For I was alive without the law once: but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the commandment, which <hi type="italic">was ordained</hi> to life, I found <hi type="italic">to be</hi> unto death. <hi type="super">11</hi> For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew <hi type="italic">me.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> Wherefore the law <hi type="italic">is</hi> holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good. <hi type="super">13</hi> Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear sin, working death in me by that which is good; that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful. 14a For we know that the law is spiritual:— <div eID="gen30608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30609" type="x-p"/> To what he had said in the former paragraph, the apostle here raises an objection, which he answers very fully: <hi type="italic">What shall we say then? Is the law sin?</hi> When he had been speaking of the dominion of sin, he had said so much of the influence of the law as a covenant upon that dominion that it might easily be misinterpreted as a reflection upon the law, to prevent which he shows from his own experience the great excellency and usefulness of the law, not as a covenant, but as a guide; and further discovers how sin took occasion by the commandment. Observe in particular, <div eID="gen30609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30610" type="x-p"/> I. The great excellency of the law in itself. Far be it from Paul to reflect upon the law; no, he speaks honourably of it. 1. It is <hi type="italic">holy, just, and good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.12">v. 12</reference>. The law in general is so, and every particular commandment is so. Laws are as the law-makers are. God, the great lawgiver, is holy, just, and good, therefore his law must needs be so. The matter of it is holy: it commands holiness, encourages holiness; it is holy, for it is agreeable to the holy will of God, the original of holiness. It is just, for it is consonant to the rules of equity and right reason: the ways of the Lord are right. It is good in the design of it; it was given for the good of mankind, for the conservation of peace and order in the world. It makes the observers of it good; the intention of it was to better and reform mankind. Wherever there is true grace there is an assent to this—that the law is holy, just, and good. 2. <hi type="italic">The law is spiritual</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.14">v. 14</reference>), not only in regard to the effect of it, as it is a means of making us spiritual, but in regard to the extent of it; it reaches our spirits, it lays a restraint upon, and gives a direction to, the motions of the inward man; <hi type="italic">it is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>. It forbids spiritual wickedness, heart-murder, and heart-adultery. It commands spiritual service, requires the heart, obliges us to worship God in the spirit. It is a spiritual law, for it is given by God, who is a Spirit and the Father of spirits; it is given to man, whose principal part is spiritual; the soul is the best part, and the leading part of the man, and therefore the law to the man must needs be a law to the soul. Herein the law of God is above all other laws, that it is a spiritual law. Other laws may forbid <hi type="italic">compassing and imagining,</hi> &c., which are treason in the heart, but cannot take cognizance thereof, unless there be some overt act; but the law of God takes notice of the iniquity regarded in the heart, though it go no further. <hi type="italic">Wash thy heart from wickedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.4.14">Jer. iv. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">We know this:</hi> Wherever there is true grace there is an experimental knowledge of the spirituality of the law of God. <div eID="gen30610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30611" type="x-p"/> II. The great advantage that he had found by the law. 1. It was discovering: <hi type="italic">I had not known sin but by the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7">v. 7</reference>. As that which is straight discovers that which is crooked, as the looking-glass shows us our natural face with all its spots and deformities, so there is no way of coming to that knowledge of sin which is necessary to repentance, and consequently to peace and pardon, but by comparing our hearts and lives with the law. Particularly he came to the knowledge of the sinfulness of lust by the law of the tenth commandment. By lust he means sin dwelling in us, sin in its first motions and workings, the corrupt principle. This he came to know when the law said, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not covet.</hi> The law spoke in other language than the scribes and Pharisees made it to speak in; it spoke in the spiritual sense and meaning of it. By this he knew that lust was sin and a very sinful sin, that those motions and desires of the heart towards sin which never came into act were sinful, exceedingly sinful. Paul had a very quick and piercing judgment, all the advantages and improvements of education, and yet never attained the right knowledge of indwelling sin till the Spirit by the law made it known to him. There is nothing about which the natural man is more blind than about original corruption, concerning which the understanding is altogether in the dark till the Spirit by the law reveal it, and make it known. Thus <hi type="italic">the law is a schoolmaster, to bring us to Christ,</hi> opens and searches the wound, and so prepares it for healing. Thus sin by the commandment does appear sin (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.13">v. 13</reference>); it appears in its own colours, appears to be what it is, and you cannot call it by a worse name than its own. Thus by the commandment it becomes <hi type="italic">exceedingly sinful;</hi> that is, it appears to be so. We never see the desperate venom or malignity there is in sin, till we come to compare it with the law, and the spiritual nature of the law, and then we see it to be an evil and a bitter thing. 2. It was humbling (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was alive.</hi> He thought himself in a very good condition; he was alive in his own opinion and apprehension, very secure and confident of the goodness of his state. Thus he was <hi type="italic">once,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pote</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">in times past,</hi> when he was a Pharisee; for it was the common temper of that generation of men that they had a very good conceit of themselves; and Paul was then like the rest of them, and the reason was he was then <hi type="italic">without the law.</hi> Though brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, though himself a great student in the law, a strict observer of it, and a zealous stickler for it, yet <hi type="italic">without the law.</hi> He had the letter of the law, but he had not the spiritual meaning of it—the shell, but not the kernel. He had the law in his hand and in his head, but he had it not in his heart; the notion of it, but not the power of it. There are a great many who are spiritually dead in sin, that yet are alive in their own opinion of themselves, and it is their strangeness to the law that is the cause of the mistake. <hi type="italic">But when the commandment came,</hi> came in the power of it (not to his eyes only, but to his heart), <hi type="italic">sin revived,</hi> as the dust in a room rises (that is, appears) when the sun-shine is let into it. Paul then saw that in sin which he had never seen before; he then saw sin in its causes, the bitter root, the corrupt bias, the bent to backslide,—sin in its colours, deforming, defiling, breaking a righteous law, affronting an awful Majesty, profaning a sovereign crown by casting it to the ground,—sin in its consequences, sin with death at the heels of it, sin and the curse entailed upon it. "Thus sin revived, and then I died; I lost that good opinion which I had had of myself, and came to be of another mind. <hi type="italic">Sin revived, and I died;</hi> that is, the Spirit, but the commandment, convinced me that I was in a state of sin, and in a state of death because of sin." Of this excellent use is the law; it is a lamp and a light; it converts the soul, opens the eyes, prepares the way of the Lord in the desert, rends the rocks, levels the mountains, makes ready a people prepared for the Lord. <div eID="gen30611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30612" type="x-p"/> III. The ill use that his corrupt nature made of the law notwithstanding. 1. <hi type="italic">Sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.8">v. 8</reference>. Observe, Paul had in him all manner of concupiscence, though one of the best unregenerate men that ever was; as touching the righteousness of the law, blameless, and yet sensible of all manner of concupiscence. And it was sin that wrought it, indwelling sin, his corrupt nature (he speaks of a sin that did work sin), and it took occasion by the commandment. The corrupt nature would not have swelled and raged so much if it had not been for the restraints of the law; as the peccant humours in the body are raised, and more inflamed, by a purge that is not strong enough to carry them off. It is incident to corrupt nature, <hi type="italic">in vetitum niti—to lean towards what is forbidden.</hi> Ever since Adam ate forbidden fruit, we have all been fond of forbidden paths; the diseased appetite is carried out most strongly towards that which is hurtful and prohibited. <hi type="italic">Without the law sin was dead,</hi> as a snake in winter, which the sunbeams of the law quicken and irritate. 2. It <hi type="italic">deceived men.</hi> Sin puts a cheat upon the sinner, and it is a fatal cheat, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.11">v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">By it</hi> (by the commandment) <hi type="italic">slew me.</hi> There being in the law no such express threatening against sinful lustings, sin, that is, his won corrupt nature, took occasion thence to promise him impunity, and to say, as the serpent to our first parents, <hi type="italic">You shall not surely die.</hi> Thus it deceived and slew him. 3. It <hi type="italic">wrought death in me by that which is good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.7.13">v. 13</reference>. That which works concupiscence works death, for sin bringeth forth death. Nothing so good but a corrupt and vicious nature will pervert it, and make it an occasion of sin; no flower so sweet by sin will such poison out of it. Now in this sin appears sin. The worst thing that sin does, and most like itself, is the perverting of the law, and taking occasion from it to be so much the more malignant. Thus the commandment, which was ordained to life, was intended as a guide in the way to comfort and happiness, proved unto death, through the corruption of nature, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.10">v. 10</reference>. Many a precious soul splits upon the rock of salvation; and the same word which to some is an occasion of life unto life is to others an occasion of death unto death. The same sun that makes the garden of flowers more fragrant makes the dunghill more noisome; the same heat that softens wax hardens clay; and the same child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel. The way to prevent this mischief is to bow our souls to the commanding authority of the word and law of God, not striving against, but submitting to it.

Same Subject Continued.</title> <div sID="gen32045" type="x-p"/> Relation of Believers to the Law and to Christ (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.1-Rom.7.6">Ro 7:1-6</reference>).<div eID="gen32045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32046" type="x-p"/> Recurring to the statement of <reference osisRef="Rom.6.14">Ro 6:14</reference>, that believers are "not under the law but under grace," the apostle here shows how this change is brought about, and what holy consequences follow from it.<div eID="gen32046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16476"/><hi type="bold">1. I speak to them that know the law--</hi>of Moses to whom, though not themselves Jews (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.1.13">Ro 1:13</reference>), the Old Testament was familiar. <div eID="gen32047" type="x-p"/>

entries.93bc51ef2bbe4a46dc220f9131d64caacdd9c3c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16479"/><div sID="gen32050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16479"/><hi type="bold">4. Wherefore ... ye also are become dead--</hi>rather, "were slain."<div eID="gen32050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the law by the body of Christ--</hi>through His slain body. The apostle here departs from his usual word "died," using the more expressive phrase "were slain," to make it clear that he meant their being "crucified with Christ" (as expressed in <reference osisRef="Rom.6.3-Rom.6.6">Ro 6:3-6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Gal.2.20">Ga 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen32051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that ye should be married to another, even to him that is--</hi>"was."<div eID="gen32052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">raised from the dead--</hi>to the intent.<div eID="gen32053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we should bring forth fruit unto God--</hi>It has been thought that the apostle should here have said that "the law died to us," not "we to the law," but that purposely inverted the figure, to avoid the harshness to Jewish ears of the death of the law [Chrysostom, Calvin, Hodge, Philippi, &c.]. But this is to mistake the apostle's design in employing this figure, which was merely to illustrate the general principle that "death dissolves legal obligation." It was essential to his argument that we, not the law, should be the dying party, since it is we that are "crucified with Christ," and not the law. This death dissolves our marriage obligation to the law, leaving us at liberty to contract a new relation--to be joined to the Risen One, in order to spiritual fruitfulness, to the glory of God [Beza, Olshausen, Meyer, Alford, &c.]. The confusion, then, is in the expositors, not the text; and it has arisen from not observing that, like Jesus Himself, believers are here viewed as having a double life--the old sin-condemned life, which they lay down with Christ, and the new life of acceptance and holiness to which they rise with their Surety and Head; and all the issues of this new life, in Christian obedience, are regarded as the "fruit" of this blessed union to the Risen One. How such holy fruitfulness was impossible before our union to Christ, is next declared. <div eID="gen32054" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c9981c84cb9689fdfb50db991c49a707d6e9e9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16480"/><div sID="gen32055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16480"/><hi type="bold">5. For when we were in the flesh--</hi>in our unregenerate state, as we came into the world. See on <reference osisRef="John.3.6">Joh 3:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rom.8.5-Rom.8.9">Ro 8:5-9</reference>.<div eID="gen32055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the motions--</hi>"passions" (Margin), "affections" (as in <reference osisRef="Gal.5.24">Ga 5:24</reference>), or "stirrings."<div eID="gen32056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of sins--</hi>that is, "prompting to the commission of sins."<div eID="gen32057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which were by the law--</hi>by occasion of the law, which fretted, irritated our inward corruption by its prohibitions. See on <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7-Rom.7.9">Ro 7:7-9</reference>.<div eID="gen32058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">did work in our members--</hi>the members of the body, as the instruments by which these inward stirrings find vent in action, and become facts of the life. See on <reference osisRef="Rom.6.6">Ro 6:6</reference>.<div eID="gen32059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to bring forth fruit unto death--</hi>death in the sense of <reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Ro 6:21</reference>. Thus hopeless is all holy fruit before union to Christ. <div eID="gen32060" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c14ce8ed34cf01480e3ab696069ec7668776063: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16481"/><div sID="gen32061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16481"/><hi type="bold">6. But now--</hi>On the same expression, see on <reference osisRef="Rom.6.22">Ro 6:22</reference>, and compare <reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">Jas 1:15</reference>.<div eID="gen32061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we are delivered from the law--</hi>The word is the same which, in <reference osisRef="Rom.6.6">Ro 6:6</reference> and elsewhere, is rendered "destroyed," and is but another way of saying (as in <reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">Ro 7:4</reference>) that "we were slain to the law by the body of Christ"; language which, though harsh to the ear, is designed and fitted to impress upon the reader the violence of that death of the Cross, by which, as by a deadly wrench, we are "delivered from the law."<div eID="gen32062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that being dead wherein we were held--</hi>It is now universally agreed that the true reading here is, "being dead to that wherein we were held." The received reading has no authority whatever, and is inconsistent with the strain of the argument; for the death spoken of, as we have seen, is not the law's, but ours, through union with the crucified Saviour.<div eID="gen32063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we should--</hi>"so as to" or "so that we."<div eID="gen32064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">serve in newness of spirit--</hi>"in the newness of the spirit."<div eID="gen32065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and not in the oldness of the letter--</hi>not in our old way of literal, mechanical obedience to the divine law, as a set of external rules of conduct, and without any reference to the state of our hearts; but in that new way of spiritual obedience which, through union to the risen Saviour, we have learned to render (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Ro 2:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2Co 3:6</reference>).<div eID="gen32066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32067" type="x-p"/> False Inferences regarding the Law Repelled (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.7-Rom.7.25">Ro 7:7-25</reference>).<div eID="gen32067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32068" type="x-p"/> And first, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7-Rom.7.13">Ro 7:7-13</reference>, in the case of the UNREGENERATE. <div eID="gen32068" type="x-p"/>
entries.d29c6ad4f31eda449702be1cfcc3902e2994a4c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16482"/><div sID="gen32069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16482"/><hi type="bold">7-8. What ... then? Is the law sin? God forbid!--</hi>"I have said that when we were in the flesh the law stirred our inward corruption, and was thus the occasion of deadly fruit: Is then the law to blame for this? Far from us be such a thought."<div eID="gen32069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Nay--</hi>"On the contrary" (as in <reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Ro 8:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.22">1Co 12:22</reference>; Greek).<div eID="gen32070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I had not known sin but by the law--</hi>It is important to fix what is meant by "sin" here. It certainly is not "the general nature of sin" [Alford, &c.], though it be true that this is learned from the law; for such a sense will not suit what is said of it in the following verses, where the meaning is the same as here. The only meaning which suits all that is said of it in this place is "the principle of sin in the heart of fallen man." The sense, then, is this: "It was by means of the law that I came to know what a virulence and strength of sinful propensity I had within me." The existence of this it did not need the law to reveal to him; for even the heathens recognized and wrote of it. But the dreadful nature and desperate power of it the law alone discovered--in the way now to be described.<div eID="gen32071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for I had not known lust, except, &c.--</hi>Here the same Greek word is unfortunately rendered by three different English ones--"lust"; "covet"; "concupiscence" (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.8">Ro 7:8</reference>)--which obscures the meaning. By using the word "lust" only, in the wide sense of all "irregular desire," or every outgoing of the heart towards anything forbidden, the sense will best be brought out; thus, "For I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not lust; But sin, taking ('having taken') occasion by the commandment (that one which forbids it), wrought in me all manner of lusting." This gives a deeper view of the tenth commandment than the mere words suggest. The apostle saw in it the prohibition not only of desire after certain things there specified, \ <hi type="bold">but of "desire after everything divinely forbidden"; in other words, all "lusting" or "irregular desire." It was this which "he had not known but by the law." The law forbidding all such desire so stirred his corruption that it wrought in him "all manner of lusting"--</hi>desire of every sort after what was forbidden. <div eID="gen32072" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9f9f2ccbf84316f8b5fe02f96a84a0510989b0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16484"/><div sID="gen32076" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16484"/><hi type="bold">9. For I was alive without the law once--</hi>"In the days of my ignorance, when, in this sense, a stranger to the law, I deemed myself a righteous man, and, as such, entitled to life at the hand of God."<div eID="gen32076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but when the commandment came--</hi>forbidding all irregular desire; for the apostle sees in this the spirit of the whole law.<div eID="gen32077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin revived--</hi>"came to life"; in its malignity and strength it unexpectedly revealed itself, as if sprung from the dead.<div eID="gen32078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and I died--</hi>"saw myself, in the eye of a law never kept and not to be kept, a dead man." <div eID="gen32079" type="x-p"/>

And--</hi>thus.<div eID="gen32080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the commandment, which was, &c.--</hi>designed<div eID="gen32081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to--</hi>give<div eID="gen32082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">life--</hi>through the keeping of it.<div eID="gen32083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I found to be unto death--</hi>through breaking it.<div eID="gen32084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For sin--</hi>my sinful nature.<div eID="gen32085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me--</hi>or "seduced me"--drew me aside into the very thing which the commandment forbade.<div eID="gen32086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and by it slew me--</hi>"discovered me to myself to be a condemned and gone man" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.7.9">Ro 7:9</reference>, "I died"). <div eID="gen32087" type="x-p"/>

Wherefore--</hi>"So that."<div eID="gen32088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the law is--</hi>"is indeed"<div eID="gen32089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good, and the commandment--</hi>that one so often referred to, which forbids all lusting.<div eID="gen32090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32091" type="x-p"/> holy, and just, and good. <div eID="gen32091" type="x-p"/>
entries.038c9d2949f236b57069d1d203e805c2a5288adf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16488"/><div sID="gen32098" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16488"/><hi type="bold">14. For we know that the law is spiritual--</hi>in its demands.<div eID="gen32098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but I am carnal--</hi>fleshly (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Ro 7:5</reference>), and as such, incapable of yielding spiritual obedience.<div eID="gen32099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sold under sin--</hi>enslaved to it. The "I" here, though of course not the regenerate, is neither the unregenerate, but the sinful principle of the renewed man, as is expressly stated in <reference osisRef="Rom.7.18">Ro 7:18</reference>. <div eID="gen32100" type="x-p"/>
entries.add0af634b7ec38214b19fac77166936840607c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16489"/><div sID="gen32101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16489"/><hi type="bold">15-16. For, &c.--</hi>better, "For that which I do I know not"; that is, "In obeying the impulses of my carnal nature I act the slave of another will than my own as a renewed man?"<div eID="gen32101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for, &c.--</hi>rather, "for not what I would (wish, desire) that do I, but what I hate that I do." <div eID="gen32102" type="x-p"/>
entries.431b27e8dbcc266147cbc0f3c34721b3ba3be377: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16491"/><div sID="gen32105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16491"/><hi type="bold">17. Now then it is no more I--</hi>my renewed self.<div eID="gen32105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that do it--</hi>"that work it."<div eID="gen32106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but sin which dwelleth in me--</hi>that principle of sin that still has its abode in me. To explain this and the following statements, as many do (even Bengel and Tholuck), of the sins of unrenewed men against their better convictions, is to do painful violence to the apostle's language, and to affirm of the unregenerate what is untrue. That coexistence and mutual hostility of "flesh" and "spirit" in the same renewed man, which is so clearly taught in <reference osisRef="Rom.8.4">Ro 8:4</reference>, &c., and in <reference osisRef="Gal.5.16">Ga 5:16</reference>, &c., is the true and only key to the language of this and the following verses. (It is hardly necessary to say that the apostle means not to disown the blame of yielding to his corruptions, by saying, "it is not he that does it, but sin that dwelleth in him." Early heretics thus abused his language; but the whole strain of the passage shows that his sole object in thus expressing himself was to bring more vividly before his readers the conflict of two opposite principles, and how entirely, as a new man--honoring from his inmost soul the law of God--he condemned and renounced his corrupt nature, with its affections and lusts, its stirrings and its outgoings, root and branch). <div eID="gen32107" type="x-p"/>
entries.32838151244f344367cc0f9057c494c396aa77fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16492"/><div sID="gen32108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16492"/><hi type="bold">18. For, &c.--</hi>better, "For I know that there dwelleth not in me, that is in my flesh, any good."<div eID="gen32108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for to will--</hi>"desire."<div eID="gen32109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is present with me; but how to perform that which is good--</hi>the supplement "how," in our version, weakens the statement.<div eID="gen32110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I find not--</hi>Here, again, we have the double self of the renewed man; "In me dwelleth no good; but this corrupt self is not my true self; it is but sin dwelling in my real self, as a renewed man." <div eID="gen32111" type="x-p"/>
entries.002e2b61ea1df8f39c3a1a352b32af4c5573d1c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16493"/><div sID="gen32112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16493"/><hi type="bold">19-21. For, &c.--</hi>The conflict here graphically described between a self that "desires" to do good and a self that in spite of this does evil, cannot be the struggles between conscience and passion in the unregenerate, because the description given of this "desire to do good" in <reference osisRef="Rom.7.22">Ro 7:22</reference> is such as cannot be ascribed, with the least show of truth, to any but the renewed. <div eID="gen32112" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5e437654c97a1964ec541a2cd85b62c92d1283a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16494"/><div sID="gen32113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16494"/><hi type="bold">22. For I delight in the law of God after the inward man--</hi>"from the bottom of my heart." The word here rendered "delight" is indeed stronger than "consent" in <reference osisRef="Rom.7.16">Ro 7:16</reference>; but both express a state of mind and heart to which the unregenerate man is a stranger. <div eID="gen32113" type="x-p"/>
entries.99643841829fa289cf3c9157a8c8185493044618: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16495"/><div sID="gen32114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16495"/><hi type="bold">23. But I see another--</hi>it should be "a different"<div eID="gen32114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law in my members--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Ro 7:5</reference>).<div eID="gen32115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members--</hi>In this important verse, observe, first, that the word "law" means an inward principle of action, good or evil, operating with the fixedness and regularity of a law. The apostle found two such laws within him; the one "the law of sin in his members," called (in <reference osisRef="Gal.5.17">Ga 5:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.5.24">24</reference>) "the flesh which lusteth against the spirit," "the flesh with the affections and lusts," that is, the sinful principle in the regenerate; the other, "the law of the mind," or the holy principle of the renewed nature. Second, when the apostle says he "sees" the one of these principles "warring against" the other, and "bringing him into captivity" to itself, he is not referring to any actual rebellion going on within him while he was writing, or to any captivity to his own lusts then existing. He is simply describing the two conflicting principles, and pointing out what it was the inherent property of each to aim at bringing about. Third, when the apostle describes himself as "brought into captivity" by the triumph of the sinful principle of his nature, he clearly speaks in the person of a renewed man. Men do not feel themselves to be in captivity in the territories of their own sovereign and associated with their own friends, breathing a congenial atmosphere, and acting quite spontaneously. But here the apostle describes himself, when drawn under the power of his sinful nature, as forcibly seized and reluctantly dragged to his enemy's camp, from which he would gladly make his escape. This ought to settle the question, whether he is here speaking as a regenerate man or the reverse. <div eID="gen32116" type="x-p"/>
entries.7460be8bb1109b78cd7eb5cdb4a20527aa069ecf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16496"/><div sID="gen32117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16496"/><hi type="bold">24. O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?--</hi>The apostle speaks of the "body" here with reference to "the law of sin" which he had said was "in his members," but merely as the instrument by which the sin of the heart finds vent in action, and as itself the seat of the lower appetites (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.6.6">Ro 6:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Ro 7:5</reference>); and he calls it "the body of this death," as feeling, at the moment when he wrote, the horrors of that death (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.21">Ro 6:21</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Ro 7:5</reference>) into which it dragged him down. But the language is not that of a sinner newly awakened to the sight of his lost state; it is the cry of a living but agonized believer, weighed down under a burden which is not himself, but which he longs to shake off from his renewed self. Nor does the question imply ignorance of the way of relief at the time referred to. It was designed only to prepare the way for that outburst of thankfulness for the divinely provided remedy which immediately follows. <div eID="gen32117" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2a77d87f5887ef7502b2750f9cef562de75519d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16497"/><div sID="gen32118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16497"/><hi type="bold">25. I thank God--</hi>the Source.<div eID="gen32118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through Jesus Christ--</hi>the Channel of deliverance.<div eID="gen32119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">So then--</hi>to sum up the whole matter.<div eID="gen32120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the mind--</hi>the mind indeed.<div eID="gen32121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I myself serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin--</hi>"Such then is the unchanging character of these two principles within me. God's holy law is dear to my renewed mind, and has the willing service of my new man; although that corrupt nature which still remains in me listens to the dictates of sin."<div eID="gen32122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Note, (1) This whole chapter was of essential service to the Reformers in their contendings with the Church of Rome. When the divines of that corrupt church, in a Pelagian spirit, denied that the sinful principle in our fallen nature, which they called "Concupiscence," and which is commonly called "Original Sin," had the nature of sin at all, they were triumphantly answered from this chapter, where--</hi>both in the first section of it, which speaks of it in the unregenerate, and in the second, which treats of its presence and actings in believers--it is explicitly, emphatically, and repeatedly called "sin." As such, they held it to be damnable. (See the Confessions both of the Lutheran and Reformed churches). In the following century, the orthodox in Holland had the same controversy to wage with "the Remonstrants" (the followers of Arminius), and they waged it on the field of this chapter. (2) Here we see that Inability is consistent with Accountability. (See <reference osisRef="Rom.7.18">Ro 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.17">Ga 5:17</reference>). "As the Scriptures constantly recognize the truth of these two things, so are they constantly united in Christian experience. Everyone feels that he cannot do the things that he would, yet is sensible that he is guilty for not doing them. Let any man test his power by the requisition to love God perfectly at all times. Alas! how entire our inability! Yet how deep our self-loathing and self-condemnation!" [Hodge]. (3) If the first sight of the Cross by the eye of faith kindles feelings never to be forgotten, and in one sense never to be repeated--like the first view of an enchanting landscape--the experimental discovery, in the latter stages of the Christian life, of its power to beat down and mortify inveterate corruption, to cleanse and heal from long-continued backslidings and frightful inconsistencies, and so to triumph over all that threatens to destroy those for whom Christ died, as to bring them safe over the tempestuous seas of this life into the haven of eternal rest--is attended with yet more heart--affecting wonder draws forth deeper thankfulness, and issues in more exalted adoration of Him whose work Salvation is from first to last (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Ro 7:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">25</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.4">4</reference>) It is sad when such topics as these are handled as mere questions of biblical interpretation or systematic theology. Our great apostle could not treat of them apart from personal experience, of which the facts of his own life and the feelings of his own soul furnished him with illustrations as lively as they were apposite. When one is unable to go far into the investigation of indwelling sin, without breaking out into an, "O wretched man that I am!" and cannot enter on the way of relief without exclaiming "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord," he will find his meditations rich in fruit to his own soul, and may expect, through Him who presides in all such matters, to kindle in his readers or hearers the like blessed emotions (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.24">Ro 7:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">25</reference>). So be it even now, O Lord! <chapter eID="Rom.7"/>

entries.096f2667651042d2378cc720dd816012ba0ad1e1: <div eID="gen46350" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen46351" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46352" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46352" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46351" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46353" type="x-p"/> The law has power over a man as long as he lives, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.1">Rom 7:1</reference>. And a wife is bound to her husband only as long as he lives, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.2">Rom 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.3">Rom 7:3</reference>. Christian believers are delivered from the Mosaic law by Christ Jesus, and united to God, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5-Rom.7.7">Rom 7:5-7</reference>. By the law is the knowledge of sin, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.8">Rom 7:8</reference>. But it gives no power over it, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.9-Rom.7.11">Rom 7:9-11</reference>. Yet it is holy, just, and good, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.12">Rom 7:12</reference>. How it convinces of sin, and brings into bondage, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.13-Rom.7.24">Rom 7:13-24</reference>. No deliverance from its curse but by Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">Rom 7:25</reference>. <div eID="gen46353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46354" type="x-p"/> The apostle having, in the preceding chapter, shown the converted Gentiles the obligations they were under to live a holy life, addresses himself here to the Jews who might hesitate to embrace the Gospel; lest, by this means, they should renounce the law, which might appear to them as a renunciation of their allegiance to God. As they rested in the law, as sufficient for justification and sanctification, it was necessary to convince them of their mistake. That the law was insufficient for their justification the apostle had proved, in chapters iii., iv., and v.; that it is insufficient for their sanctification he shows in this chapter; and introduces his discourse by showing that a believing Jew is discharged from his obligations to the law, and is at liberty to come under another and much happier constitution, viz. that of the Gospel of Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.1-Rom.7.4">Rom 7:1-4</reference>. In <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Rom 7:5</reference> he gives a general description of the state of a Jew, in servitude to sin, considered as under mere law. In <reference osisRef="Rom.7.6">Rom 7:6</reference> he gives a summary account of the state of a Christian, or believing Jew, and the advantages he enjoys under the Gospel. Upon <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Rom 7:5</reference> he comments, from Romans 7:7-25, and upon <reference osisRef="Rom.7.6">Rom 7:6</reference> he comments, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1-Rom.8.11">Rom 8:1-11</reference>. <div eID="gen46354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46355" type="x-p"/> In explaining his position in <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Rom 7:5</reference> he shows: <div eID="gen46355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46356" type="x-p"/> 1. That the law reaches to all the branches and latent principles of sin, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7">Rom 7:7</reference>. <div eID="gen46356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46357" type="x-p"/> 2. That it subjected the sinner to death, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.8-Rom.7.12">Rom 7:8-12</reference>, without the expectation of pardon. <div eID="gen46357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46358" type="x-p"/> 3. He shows the reason why the Jew was put under it, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.13">Rom 7:13</reference>. <div eID="gen46358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46359" type="x-p"/> 4. He proves that the law, considered as a rule of action, though it was spiritual, just, holy, and good in itself, yet was insufficient for sanctification, or for freeing a man from the power of inbred sin. <div eID="gen46359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46360" type="x-p"/> For, as the prevalency of sensual appetites cannot wholly extinguish the voice of reason and conscience, a man may acknowledge the law to be holy, just, and good, and yet his passions reign within him, keeping him in the most painful and degrading servitude, while the law supplied no power to deliver him from them, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.14-Rom.7.24">Rom 7:14-24</reference>, as that power can only be supplied by the grace of Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">Rom 7:25</reference>. See Taylor. <div eID="gen46360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46361" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen46361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46362" type="x-p"/> For I speak to them that know the law - This is a proof that the apostle directs this part of his discourse to the Jews. <div eID="gen46362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46363" type="x-p"/> As long as he liveth? - Or, as long as It liveth; law does not extend its influence to the dead, nor do abrogated laws bind. It is all the same whether we understand these words as speaking of a law abrogated, so that it cannot command; or of its objects being dead, so that it has none to bind. In either case the law has no force.
entries.d0da169fa0d9095faeed8ef7877fd78267d39421: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen46363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46364" type="x-p"/> For the woman which hath a husband - The apostle illustrates his meaning by a familiar instance. A married woman is bound to her husband while he lives; but when her husband is dead she is discharged from the law by which she was bound to him alone.
entries.3bb8f901a3dcc60c96befbcbdd36bd280e1c3899: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen46364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46365" type="x-p"/> So then, if, while her husband liveth - The object of the apostle's similitude is to show that each party is equally bound to the other; but that the death of either dissolves the engagement. <div eID="gen46365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46366" type="x-p"/> So - she is no adulteress, though she be married to another - And do not imagine that this change would argue any disloyalty in you to your Maker; for, as he has determined that this law of ordinances shall cease, you are no more bound to it than a woman is to a deceased husband, and are as free to receive the Gospel of Christ as a woman in such circumstances would be to remarry.
entries.3e4c0d53cae9660b256a05d9fe3b4e7c4b59d861: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen46366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46367" type="x-p"/> Wherefore, my brethren - This is a parallel case. You were once under the law of Moses, and were bound by its injunctions; but now ye are become dead to that law - a modest, inoffensive mode of speech, for, The law, which was once your husband, is dead; God has determined that it shall be no longer in force; so that now, as a woman whose husband is dead is freed from the law of that husband, or from her conjugal vow, and may legally be married to another, so God, who gave the law under which ye have hitherto lived, designed that it should be in force only till the advent of the Messiah; that advent has taken place, the law has consequently ceased, and now ye are called to take on you the yoke of the Gospel, and lay down the yoke of the law; and it is the design of God that you should do so. <div eID="gen46367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46368" type="x-p"/> That ye should be married to another - who is raised from the dead - As Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth, the object of God in giving the law was to unite you to Christ; and, as he has died, he has not only abolished that law which condemns every transgressor to death, without any hope of a revival, but he has also made that atonement for sin, by his own death, which is represented in the sacrifices prescribed by the law. And as Jesus Christ is risen again from the dead, he has thereby given the fullest proof that by his death he has procured the resurrection of mankind, and made that atonement required by the law. That we should bring forth fruit unto God - we, Jews, who believe in Christ, have, in consequence of our union with him, received the gifts and graces of the Holy Spirit; so that we bring forth that fruit of holiness unto God which, without this union, it would be impossible for us to produce. Here is a delicate allusion to the case of a promising and numerous progeny from a legitimate and happy marriage.
entries.9c80dd3f95915dc05b02280b5967ed40a2568d29: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen46368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46369" type="x-p"/> For, when we were in the flesh - When we were without the Gospel, in our carnal and unregenerated state, though believing in the law of Moses, and performing the rites and offices of our religion. <div eID="gen46369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46370" type="x-p"/> The motions of sins, which were by the law - Τα παθηματα των ἁμαρτιων, the passions of sins, the evil propensities to sins; to every particular sin there is a propensity: one propensity does not excite to all kinds of sinful acts; hence the apostle uses the plural number, the Passions or propensities of Sins; sins being not more various than their propensities in the unregenerate heart, which excite to them. These παθηματα, propensities, constitute the fallen nature; they are the disease of the heart, the pollution and corruption of the soul. <div eID="gen46370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46371" type="x-p"/> Did work in our members - The evil propensity acts εν τοις μελεσιν, in the whole nervous and muscular system, applying that stimulus to every part which is necessary to excite them to action. <div eID="gen46371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46372" type="x-p"/> To bring forth fruit unto death - To produce those acts of transgression which subject the sinner to death, temporal and eternal. When the apostle says, the motion of sin which were by the law, he points out a most striking and invariable characteristic of sin, viz. its rebellious nature; it ever acts against law, and the most powerfully against known law. Because the law requires obedience, therefore it will transgress. The law is equally against evil passions and evil actions, and both these exert themselves against it. So, these motions which were by the law, became roused into the most powerful activity by the prohibitions of the law. They were comparatively dormant till the law said, thou shalt Not do this, thou shalt Do that; then the rebellious principle in the evil propensity became roused, and acts of transgression and omissions of duty were the immediate consequences.
entries.a68cd4b38b47f4717a881bb39221030238debef0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen46372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46373" type="x-p"/> But now we are delivered from the law - We, who have believed in Christ Jesus, are delivered from that yoke by which we were bound, which sentenced every transgressor to perdition, but provided no pardon even for the penitent, and no sanctification for those who are weary of their inbred corruptions. <div eID="gen46373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46374" type="x-p"/> That being dead wherein we were held - To us believers in Christ this commandment is abrogated; we are transferred to another constitution; that law which kills ceases to bind us; it is dead to us who have believed in Christ Jesus, who is the end of the law for justification and salvation to every one that believes. <div eID="gen46374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46375" type="x-p"/> That we should serve in newness of spirit - We are now brought under a more spiritual dispensation; now we know the spiritual import of all the Mosaic precepts. We see that the law referred to the Gospel, and can only be fulfilled by the Gospel. <div eID="gen46375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46376" type="x-p"/> The oldness of the letter - The merely literal rites, ceremonies, and sacrifices are now done away; and the newness of the spirit, the true intent and meaning of all are now fully disclosed; so that we are got from an imperfect state into a state of perfection and excellence. We sought justification and sanctification, pardon and holiness, by the law, and have found that the law could not give them: we have sought these in the Gospel scheme, and we have found them. We serve God now, not according to the old literal sense, but in the true spiritual meaning.
entries.4a3d967d37ac2d92e535713d8569ae1107d2be83: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen46376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46377" type="x-p"/> Is the law sin? - The apostle had said, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.6">Rom 7:6</reference> : The motions of sins, which were by the law, did bring forth fruit unto death; and now he anticipates an objection, "Is therefore the law sin?" To which he answers, as usual, μη γενοιτο, by no means. Law is only the means of disclosing; this sinful propensity, not of producing it; as a bright beam of the sun introduced into a room shows; millions of motes which appear to be dancing in it in all directions; but these were not introduced by the light: they were there before, only there was not light enough to make them manifest; so the evil propensity was there before, but there was not light sufficient to discover it. <div eID="gen46377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46378" type="x-p"/> I had not known sin, but by the law - Mr. Locke and Dr. Taylor have properly remarked the skill used by St. Paul in dexterously avoiding, as much as possible, the giving offense to the Jews: and this is particularly evident in his use of the word I in this place. In the beginning of the chapter, where he mentions their knowledge of the law, he says Ye; in the 4th verse he joins himself with them, and says we; but here, and so to the end of the chapter, where he represents the power of sin and the inability of the law to subdue it, he appears to leave them out, and speaks altogether in the first person, though it is plain he means all those who are under the law. So, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.7">Rom 3:7</reference>, he uses the singular pronoun, why am I judged a sinner? when he evidently means the whole body of unbelieving Jews. <div eID="gen46378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46379" type="x-p"/> There is another circumstance in which his address is peculiarly evident; his demonstrating the insufficiency of the law under color of vindicating it. He knew that the Jew would take fire at the least reflection on the law, which he held in the highest veneration; and therefore he very naturally introduces him catching at that expression, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Rom 7:5</reference>, the motions of sins, which were by the law, or, notwithstanding the law. "What!" says this Jew, "do you vilify the law, by charging it with favoring sin?" By no means, says the apostle; I am very far from charging the law with favoring sin. The law is holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.12">Rom 7:12</reference>. Thus he writes in vindication of the law; and yet at the same time shows: <div eID="gen46379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46380" type="x-p"/> 1. That the law requires the most extensive obedience, discovering and condemning sin in all its most secret and remote branches, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.7">Rom 7:7</reference>. <div eID="gen46380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46381" type="x-p"/> 2. That it gives sin a deadly force, subjecting every transgression to the penalty of death, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.8-Rom.7.14">Rom 7:8-14</reference>. And yet, <div eID="gen46381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46382" type="x-p"/> 3. supplies neither help nor hope to the sinner, but leaves him under the power of sin, and the sentence of death, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.14">Rom 7:14</reference>, etc. This, says Dr. Taylor, is the most ingenious turn of writing I ever met with. We have another instance of the same sort, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1-Rom.13.7">Rom 13:1-7</reference>. <div eID="gen46382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46383" type="x-p"/> It is not likely that a dark, corrupt human heart can discern the will of God. His law is his will. It recommends what is just, and right, and good and forbids what is improper, unjust, and injurious. If God had not revealed himself by this law, we should have done precisely what many nations of the earth have done, who have not had this revelation - put darkness for light, and sin for acts of holiness. While the human heart is its own measure it will rate its workings according to its own propensities; for itself is its highest rule. But when God gives a true insight of his own perfections, to be applied as a rule both of passion and practice, then sin is discovered, and discovered too, to be exceedingly sinful. So strong propensities, because they appear to be inherent in our nature, would have passed for natural and necessary operations; and their sinfulness would not have been discovered, if the law had not said, Thou shalt not covet; and thus determined that the propensity itself, as well as its outward operations, is sinful. The law is the straight edge which determines the quantum of obliquity in the crooked line to which it is applied. <div eID="gen46383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46384" type="x-p"/> It is natural for man to do what is unlawful, and to desire especially to do that which is forbidden. The heathens have remarked this propensity in man. <div eID="gen46384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46385" type="x-p"/> Thus Livy, xxxiv. 4: - <div eID="gen46385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46386" type="x-p"/> Luxuria - ipsis vinculis, sicut fera bestia, irtitata. "Luxury, like a wild beast, is irritated by its very bonds." <div eID="gen46386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46387" type="x-p"/> Audax omnia perpeti <div eID="gen46387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46388" type="x-p"/> Gens humana ruit per vetitun; nefas. "The presumptuous human race obstinately rush into prohibited acts of wickedness." <div eID="gen46388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46389" type="x-p"/> Hor. Carm. lib. i. Od. iii. ver. 25. <div eID="gen46389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46390" type="x-p"/> And Ovid, Amor. lib. ii. Eleg. xix. ver. 3: - <div eID="gen46390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46391" type="x-p"/> Quod licet, ingratum est; quod non licet, acrius urit. "What is lawful is insipid; the strongest propensity is excited towards that which is prohibited." <div eID="gen46391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46392" type="x-p"/> And again, Ib. lib. iii. E. iv. ver. 17: - <div eID="gen46392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46393" type="x-p"/> Nitimur in vetitum semper, cupimusque negata. "Vice is provoked by every strong restraint, <div eID="gen46393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46394" type="x-p"/> Sick men long most to drink, who know they mayn't." <div eID="gen46394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46395" type="x-p"/> The same poet delivers the same sentiment it another place: - <div eID="gen46395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46396" type="x-p"/> Acrior admonitu est, irritaturque retenta <div eID="gen46396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46397" type="x-p"/> Et crescit rabies: remoraminaque ipsa nocebant. <div eID="gen46397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46398" type="x-p"/> Metam. lib. iii. ver. 566. "Being admonished, he becomes the more obstinate; and his fierceness is irritated by restraints. Prohibitions become incentives to greater acts of vice." <div eID="gen46398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46399" type="x-p"/> But it is needless to multiply examples; this most wicked principle of a sinful, fallen nature, has been felt and acknowledged by All mankind.
entries.3443ac30a9f7e9758655c79c3b87826393b056a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen46399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46400" type="x-p"/> Sin, taking occasion by the commandment - I think the pointing, both in this and in the 11th verse, to be wrong: the comma should be after occasion, and not after commandment. But sin taking occasion, wrought in me by this commandment all manner of concupiscence. There are different opinions concerning the meaning of the word αφορμη, which we here translate occasion. Dr. Waterland translates the clause, Sin, taking Advantage. Dr. Taylor contends that all commentators have mistaken the meaning of it, and that it should be rendered having received Force. For this acceptation of the word I can find no adequate authority except in its etymology - απο, from, and ὁρμη, impetus. The word appears to signify, in general, whatsoever is necessary for the completion or accomplishment of any particular purpose. Xenophon uses αφορμαι εις τον βιον to signify whatever is necessary for the support of life. There is a personification in the text: sin is, represented as a murderer watching for life, and snatching at every means and embracing every opportunity to carry his fell purpose into effect. The miserable sinner has a murderer, sin, within him; this murderer can only destroy life in certain circumstances; finding that the law condemns the object of his cruelty to death, he takes occasion from this to work in the soul all manner of concupiscence, evil and irregular desires and appetites of every kind, and, by thus increasing the evil, exposes the soul to more condemnation; and thus it is represented as being slain, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.11">Rom 7:11</reference>. That is, the law, on the evidence of those sinful dispositions, and their corresponding practices, condemns the sinner to death: so that he is dead in law. Thus the very prohibition, as we have already seen in the preceding verse, becomes the instrument of exciting the evil propensity; for, although a sinner has the general propensity to do what is evil, yet he seems to feel most delight in transgressing known law: stat pro ratione voluntas; "I will do it, because I will." <div eID="gen46400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46401" type="x-p"/> For without the law, sin was dead - Where there is no law there is no transgression; for sin is the transgression of the law; and no fault can be imputed unto death, where there is no statute by which such a fault is made a capital offense. <div eID="gen46401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46402" type="x-p"/> Dr. Taylor thinks that χωρις νομου, without the law, means the time before the giving of the law from Mount Sinai, which took in the space of 430 years, during which time the people were under the Abrahamic covenant of grace; and without the law that was given on Mount Sinai, the sting of death, which is sin, had not power to slay the sinner; for, from the time that Adam sinned, the law was not re-enacted till it was given by Moses, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.13">Rom 5:13</reference>. The Jew was then alive, because he was not under the law subjecting him to death for his transgressions; but when the commandment came, with the penalty of death annexed, sin revived, and the Jew died. Then the sting of death acquired life; and the Jew, upon the first transgression, was dead in law. Thus sin, the sting of death, received force or advantage to destroy by the commandment, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.8">Rom 7:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.11">Rom 7:11</reference>. <div eID="gen46402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46403" type="x-p"/> All manner of concupiscence - It showed what was evil and forbade it; and then the principle of rebellion, which seems essential to the very nature of sins rose up against the prohibition; and he was the more strongly incited to disobey in proportion as obedience was enjoined. Thus the apostle shows that the law had authority to prohibit, condemn, and destroy; but no power to pardon sin, root out enmity, or save the soul. <div eID="gen46403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46404" type="x-p"/> The word επιθυμια, which we render concupiscence, signifies simply strong desire of any kind; but in the New Testament, it is generally taken to signify irregular and unholy desires. Sin in the mind is the desire to do, or to be, what is contrary to the holiness and authority of God. <div eID="gen46404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46405" type="x-p"/> For without the law, sin was dead - This means, according to Dr. Taylor's hypothesis, the time previous to the giving of the law. See before. But it seems also consistent with the apostle's meaning, to interpret the place as implying the time in which Paul, in his unconverted Jewish state, had not the proper knowledge of the law - while he was unacquainted with its spirituality. He felt evil desire, but he did not know the evil of it; he did not consider that the law tried the heart and its workings, as well as outward actions. This is farther explained in the next verse.
entries.0a45144a87f1318faf185bb7e6b5b1e0831ff577: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen46405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46406" type="x-p"/> I was alive without the law once - Dr. Whitby paraphrases the verse thus: - "For the seed of Abraham was alive without the law once, before the law was given, I being not obnoxious to death for that to which the law had not threatened death; but when the commandment came, forbidding it under that penalty, sin revived, and I died; i.e. it got strength to draw me to sin, and to condemn me to death. Sin is, in Scripture, represented as an enemy that seeks our ruin and destruction; and takes all occasions to effect it. It is here said to war against the mind, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.23">Rom 7:23</reference>; elsewhere, to war against the soul, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.11">1Pet 2:11</reference>; to surround and beset us, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">Heb 12:1</reference>; to bring us into bondage and subjection, and get the dominion over us, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.12">Rom 6:12</reference>; to entice us, and so to work our death, <reference osisRef="Jam.1.14-Jam.1.16">Jam 1:14-16</reference>; and to do all that Satan, the grand enemy of mankind, doth, by tempting us to the commission of it. Whence Chrysostom, upon those words, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.4">Heb 12:4</reference> : Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, προς την ἁμαρτιαν ανταγωνιζομενοι, striving against sin; represents sin as an armed and flagrant adversary. When, therefore, it finds a law which threatens death to the violator of it, it takes occasion thence more earnestly to tempt and allure to the violation of it, that so it may more effectually subject us to death and condemnation on that account; for the sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law, condemning us to death for transgressing it. Thus, when God had forbidden, on pain of death, the eating the fruit of the tree of knowledge, Satan thence took occasion to tempt our first parents to transgress, and so slew them, or made them subject to death; εξηπατησε, he deceived them, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.13">Gen 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.14">1Tim 2:14</reference>; which is the word used <reference osisRef="Rom.7.11">Rom 7:11</reference>. The phrase, without the law, sin was dead, means, that sin was then (before the law was given) comparatively dead, as to its power of condemning to death; and this sense the antithesis requires; without the law, ἁμαρτια νεκρα, εγω δε εζων, sin was dead, but I was living; but when the commandment came, (i.e. the law), sin revived, and I died. How were men living before the law, but because then no law condemned them? Sin, therefore, must be then dead, as to its condemning power. How did they die when the law came but by the law condemning them to death?
